# `star.phases()` {#fn-star-phases}

W02 replayed the Gacrux heliacal-rising date at Skorba West and passed it to the crossing and sky-reconstruction calculations. [W02 results](w02-field-to-sky.qmd).

Seasonal searches require full skyline coverage. H07 checked rejection of a partial photograph and successful calculation with the full profile. [H07 results](h07-panorama-coverage.qmd).

[Function index](function-index.html#idx-star-phases)

```{=html}
<p>Seasonal visibility depends on solar depression, stellar altitude, apparent magnitude
and atmospheric extinction as well as terrain. The model holds the star's position fixed
for the chosen year and samples a 365-day solar cycle with uniformly spaced ecliptic
longitudes. It requires a star-Sun altitude separation of 2.1 times the catalogue
magnitude plus 10 degrees, and compares extinction-adjusted magnitude with the limiting
magnitude. A positive-duration overlap of visibility conditions determines the daily
code. The stellar altitude trend within a visible interval below alt.rs determines
rising or setting. Terrain reappearance of a descending star therefore contributes
a setting phase. Disjoint runs are reported as separate seasons on the circular
model year, including runs spanning the December-solstice reference.
</p>
<p>Both constant and varying horizons are evaluated on all 365 model days. A horizon
object supplies the coordinates and piecewise-linear horizon. The profile must
cover all bearings and close at north. Use alt.hor only with coordinate input.
A fixed-coordinate stellar track is shared across model days. The terrain search
uses the same corners, azimuth reversals, interior extrema and 0.01-second root
tolerance as <code>riseset</code>, collecting all crossings during the model day.
Visible windows can lie wholly between minute samples. A touch without clearance
contributes no visible duration. Source terrain resolution and numerical tolerances
limit the shortest resolvable window.
</p>
```

<details><summary>Implementation arguments, return value and documented modes</summary>

```{=html}
<table><thead><tr><th>Argument</th><th>Formal default</th><th>Behaviour in this interface</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row"><code>star</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Either the star name or a <em>skyscapeR.star</em> object.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>year</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>The year of interest. Historical labels such as <code>"3700 BC"</code> are accepted by <code>astroYear</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>loc</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Location, either a <em>skyscapeR.horizon</em> or a vector
containing the latitude, longitude and elevation of location, in this order.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt.hor</code></th><td><code>0</code></td><td><p>The altitude of the horizon to consider.
Defaults to zero degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>alt.rs</code></th><td><code>10</code></td><td><p>The maximum altitude of a star's first or last
visibility for it to still be considered to be as rising or setting.
Defaults to ten degrees.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>solar.alt</code></th><td><code>NULL</code></td><td><p>Solar altitude threshold in degrees. NULL uses
-6 for a horizon, or alt.hor - 6 for coordinate input.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>k</code></th><td><code>skyscapeR.vars()$k</code></td><td><p>Visual extinction in magnitudes per airmass (Schaefer 1986, p. S33). The package adopts 0.2 as a clear-sky baseline. Extinction varies with site and atmospheric conditions (Schaefer 1986, 1993). Defaults to the session value from skyscapeR.vars().</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>limit</code></th><td><code>6</code></td><td><p>The maximum magnitude of a star that can be
visible with the naked eye. Defaults to 6.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>refraction</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Logical. Apply atmospheric refraction. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>atm</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Atmospheric pressure in mbar. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>temp</code></th><td>—</td><td><p>Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Defaults to the session setting in <code>skyscapeR.vars</code>.</p></td></tr><tr><th scope="row"><code>res</code></th><td><code>1/24/6</code></td><td><p>Spacing of solar altitude samples in days, greater than zero and at
most one. Default 1/144 day (ten minutes). Terrain crossings are refined separately.</p></td></tr></tbody></table><h5>Return value</h5><p>A skyscapeR.starphases list. The data table gives each model day and its phase code: I for invisible, V for visible without a classified rise or set, R for rising, S for setting and RS for both. Metadata include the star, year, observer coordinates, phase type, season and event tables, refraction setting and solar altitude threshold. For a named horizon, <code>metadata$site.name</code> retains the site label for comparisons. The logical <code>metadata$horizon</code> records whether a horizon object was supplied. The separate <code>metadata$horizon.status</code> reports <code>"always above"</code>, <code>"always below"</code> or <code>"crosses"</code> relative to the supplied skyline. Event rows include solar.longitude in degrees on the synthetic cycle. The date.julian column gives the representative local Julian calendar date at the supplied longitude. Pass this date to <code>riseset</code> with <code>calendar = "J"</code> to time the skyline crossing. For a dawn sketch, advance from that crossing until the star clears the terrain while the sky is still dark enough. The phase date alone does not specify a visible instant.
</p><h5>Extinction and model scope</h5><p>The implementation uses Rozenberg's airmass approximation,
<i>X(h)=1/(\sin h+0.025\exp(-11\sin h))</i>, multiplying it by <code>k</code>
and adding the result to the fixed catalogue magnitude. Here <code>h</code> is the
stellar altitude selected by <code>refraction</code>, above the astronomical
horizontal. This is distinct from the height above a ridge. The star-Sun
altitude-separation rule uses the catalogue magnitude before extinction.
</p><p>The model does not calculate scattered moonlight, artificial light pollution,
weather, an observer's adaptation history, or variable-star light curves.
The same separation threshold is used at all relative azimuths. It is therefore
a screening model for seasonal opportunities, not a probability of detection.
Supplying an integrated cluster entry such as M45 treats its total magnitude as
one target; cluster size, surface brightness and resolution into individual
stars do not enter this calculation. It does not predict when each Pleiad is
individually visible.
</p><p>Horizon status is determined from positive-duration clearance intervals along
the same stellar track used for the phase calculation, with the supplied
skyline and refraction setting. The same calculation applies in both
hemispheres. A track with no clearance returns an ordinary all-I result,
rather than raising an error. An always-clear track still undergoes the
extinction and solar-darkness tests; never setting does not imply visibility.
A star that never sets below a level horizontal can cross a raised ridge.
Isolated tangencies do not count as intervals of clearance or obstruction.
Numerical resolution and the supplied terrain profile limit this status.
</p><p>The separate metadata$horizon.status field is "always above", "always below"
or "crosses", relative to the supplied skyline. Phase codes R and S describe
the rising or descending part of a visible track below alt.rs; they do not
require a physical skyline crossing that day. An always-clear star may thus
have seasonal R/S codes. The type "circumpolar" is retained for an all-V
result only when the track is always above the skyline; other all-V results
are labelled "visible throughout cycle". Use horizon.status, not type, to
distinguish clearance from seasonal visibility.
</p><h5>Dates and a subsequent sky sketch</h5><p>Events follow adjacent-sample transitions around the closed cycle, including
the December-solstice boundary. Entering and leaving I mark acronycal setting
and heliacal rising; entering and leaving V mark acronycal rising and heliacal
setting. A season continuing across the boundary creates no event there.
Constant phase sequences have no transition events.
</p><p>The 365 model samples are equally spaced in solar longitude, not in elapsed
civil time. Printed seasonal labels are anchored to the December solstice.
<code>metadata$events$date.julian</code> instead solves for the event solar longitude
in the requested year and converts it to a local mean-solar Julian-calendar
date using longitude. It is a representative date, not an exact detection
instant, and can differ from the synthetic <code>day</code> label.
</p><p>Pass the representative date to <code>riseset</code> with
<code>calendar = "J"</code> and an explicit timezone. With UTC or a fixed offset,
inspect neighbouring dates when local mean-solar and civil days differ.
The returned rise is a skyline crossing. Follow it by a short time sequence
with <code>sketchSky</code> and <code>skyStep</code> to inspect terrain
clearance and the changing brightness of the local sky.
</p><p>A supplied <code>skyscapeR.star</code> is used as given. Recompute it for the requested
year; the phase function does not update an existing object's coordinates.
</p><h5>How precise is a heliacal-rising date?</h5><p>In 69 of 70 individual comparisons, the estimated first morning of visibility was within a week of the predicted heliacal-rising date.
</p><h5>Reproducing a saved result</h5><p>Metadata retain the resolved star, year, observer coordinates, extinction,
atmospheric settings and solar-altitude threshold, together with <code>limit</code>,
<code>alt.rs</code>, <code>res</code> and <code>alt.hor</code>. The latter is NA when a terrain
profile replaces the constant horizon. <code>metadata$horizon.profile</code> contains
the numerical <code>az</code>/<code>alt</code> table used, or NULL for a constant horizon.
Landscape images and DEMs are not copied into the result. Existing logical
<code>horizon</code> and <code>skyline</code> fields are retained.
</p><p><code>metadata$provenance$packages</code> records the loaded skyscapeR and swephR
versions; an unavailable version is NA, for example when sourcing functions
outside a package namespace. Version strings do not uniquely identify
development builds. Retain the original script, code revision and ephemeris
files as well: the saved metadata do not identify or archive those files.
Earlier saved results do not acquire these fields automatically.
</p>
```

</details>
